One thing I came to understand is that drug use is normal — it's a normal evolutionary impulse for human beings, we literally have to alter our consciousness in some way, and those who don't actually suffer more than those who do. The most common drugs we use to alter consciousness are tobacco, caffeine, and alcohol, and you can track the development of the use of these three drugs with the development of industrialism — we didn't start actively using these a lot until the 17th century, and use grew because these drugs supported the industrial mindset: stimulation during the day to get things done, and stimulation in the evening with alcohol to unwind. Psychedelics, more than cannabis, alcohol, caffeine, or tobacco, help with stepping back and looking at things from a broader lens. This hypothesis is rooted in a 1966 research study by Dr. James Fadiman, a psychologist — he's sort of the godfather of microdosing, talked about it on Tim Ferriss's podcast, wrote a book called The Psychedelic Explorer's Guide. In the 60s he was a leading researcher on the overlap of psychedelics and creativity and problem-solving. Bryan Fields: Why does that put them at risk?

Paul F. Austin: We all know the anecdote of Elon Musk going on Joe Rogan and smoking a blunt — maybe four or five years ago — and as a result Tesla shares dropped substantially because of potential risk with the SEC, since he was using a federally illegal drug in a legal context. Every SpaceX employee then had to get drug tested as a result, which is insane given the value of the type of cognitive work his team does — there's uncertainty on all sides but massive repercussions to decisions. Psychedelics are a slightly superior substance for that compared to cannabis, which can become more of an everyday habit rather than something done occasionally — when done occasionally cannabis can have a very psychedelic effect and substantially help with creativity, but with consistent use I lose some of that impact. Elon was recently interviewed by Don Lemon and was open that he uses ketamine here and there for depression, which is a legal substance prescribed by a medical professional, so there's more capacity now for leaders to talk openly about ketamine use specifically. The challenge is that until legal structure and policy change more substantially, the risk isn't worth it for most. I do think it's critical that the leaders, creators, and builders of tomorrow are informed and influenced by psychedelics — my hypothesis is that the more leaders who work with psychedelics, the better society becomes for everyone.

Kellan: I've always had a question — psychedelics is a broad description of multiple drugs. Is there a purpose a CEO may use magic mushrooms over LSD from a microdosing standpoint — would they choose based on what they're trying to achieve?

Paul F. Austin: Yeah, the protocol they're looking for. I had a tweet the other day — psychedelic comes from a Greek word meaning "mind manifesting," really "soul manifesting" — psyche is Greek for mind, and the Greeks perceived the mind as also part of the soul, which is what Plato talked about with duality. Delos means to manifest. The term was coined in the early 1960s by Aldous Huxley and a psychiatrist named Humphry Osmond, who guided Huxley through his first psychedelic experience. They were focused on three main classes of drugs: tryptamines — DMT, psilocybin, ayahuasca, 5-MeO-DMT; lysergamides — LSD is the most well known; and phenethylamines — the two most common being mescaline, which is in San Pedro and peyote, and MDMA is also a phenethylamine. Ketamine doesn't fall within that, cannabis doesn't, ibogaine doesn't, so there's a lot of questions about what is and isn't a psychedelic. The context of why someone is coming into this and where they're at matters a lot. The metaphor I teach in our training program is the lotus flower metaphor — the lotus represents enlightenment in Buddhism. We plant a new seed of self through a high-dose psychedelic experience, but for that to be successful we need healthy soil — tilling the soil means trauma work, healing work, shadow work. Once that's done, planting the new seed of self is the death-and-rebirth, ego-dissolution aspect. Once planted, we need to nourish that seed with exercise, meditation, diet, lifestyle practices — that's integration. Then things like ayahuasca, 5-MeO, and potentially ibogaine help the lotus flower fully blossom. Regardless of leadership position, people new to psychedelic or inner work usually need some initial tilling — trauma work — even without a big-T trauma. I count myself fortunate that I wasn't emotionally or sexually abused, had reasonably good parenting, but I was bullied quite a bit around 10-12, which is where some of my trauma came from — I can be prickly, not all that social, prefer to be introverted. Even so, in my early psychedelic work guilt, shame, and attachment issues came up that I had to navigate through a more therapeutic process. So often the first step, even for high-functioning people without a diagnosis, is that tilling — usually with ketamine or MDMA, which are a bit less intense than five grams of mushrooms in the dark. Once the soil is tilled, a high dose of psilocybin can be a great way to do the death-and-rebirth, plant the new seed of self — could also be a high dose of LSD, but people have a harder time finding it and some are still scared of it due to 1950s-60s stigma, so usually a high dose of psilocybin works well. Then microdosing in the week to four weeks after elongates the window of neuroplasticity — that's why psychedelics can be so effective at catalyzing behavioral change. Normally people find two to three weeks post-high-dose experience where things feel more in flow, they're kinder, more compassionate, more relational, but after two to three weeks that starts to dissipate. Microdosing can elongate that window to six to eight weeks, which is roughly the amount of time needed to establish a new habit. On LSD versus psilocybin specifically from a neurochemistry standpoint: tryptamines are more serotonergic — serotonin relates to contentment, present emotion, somatic experience; lysergamides are more dopaminergic — dopamine relates to focus, attention, motivation. Folks interested in psilocybin often have a history of SSRI use and want something natural to reconnect with their body. Folks interested in microdosing LSD often want to be more in flow, have greater cognitive capacity, be creative — for cognition, LSD is superior because of its dopamine impact. Compared to Adderall or Vyvanse, which bring constriction and intensity and can leave you feeling hungover, LSD microdosing retains playfulness while still getting things done.

Kellan: What are the steps someone should take to establish a protocol, or for a retreat in general?

Paul F. Austin: Going back to the lotus flower metaphor over a five-to-ten-year trajectory — you might start with MDMA-assisted or ketamine-assisted psychotherapy for six months to eighteen months, then move to a high dose of psilocybin on a retreat in Mexico or Oregon depending on legality, and then substances like ayahuasca — I didn't drink ayahuasca until I'd been working with psychedelics for seven years. There's a necessity in being patient with the path; a lot of people rush in because they hear how impactful psychedelics can be. I coach folks to take it slow, be intentional, find great providers, and commit to facing all aspects of who they are. Neuroplasticity is a huge benefit, especially for leaders and creators, but just as important is a sense of courage that comes from deep psychedelic work — psychedelics downregulate the amygdala, the reptilian brain, where a lot of our fear response comes from, opening space to ask hard questions, make difficult decisions, have difficult conversations while staying regulated. There's a quote — maybe Jim Rohn — about the quality of your life being dictated by your willingness to have difficult conversations, and psychedelics often help with that while staying compassionate.

Kellan: If someone wants to go on a retreat, what's the prep work like, and how do they approach the whole situation?

Paul F. Austin: There are three main options. One is to do it at home with virtual support — when COVID hit, the federal government passed the Ryan Haight Act allowing scheduled substances to be prescribed virtually, specifically for ADHD medication but also applied to ketamine, so over the last four years hundreds of thousands of people have worked with ketamine virtually, sent to your house after a consultation and prescription, with a trip sitter who could just be a friend, and virtual coaching before and after. We offer that through Third Wave — a two-month personalized psychedelic coaching program guiding a high-dose experience followed by a microdosing protocol with coaching support, all from the comfort of your own home, which matters because set and setting are so important. The second common way is to go on a retreat in a legal place — the Netherlands, Jamaica, Costa Rica, Mexico, now Oregon since it legalized psilocybin, and Colorado. We have a directory of vetted retreat centers at thethirdwave.co, whether it's ayahuasca, psilocybin, ketamine, or huachuma. That can cost anywhere from a thousand to eleven thousand dollars depending on the center, typically with four to six weeks of group preparation calls beforehand and four to six weeks of integration calls after, with optional one-on-one support. The third way is to find an underground community — plant medicine circles happening every weekend in places like New York, illegal in most states but legal in Colorado. Law enforcement generally isn't interested in prosecuting psychedelic work, partly because half of police forces have worked with psychedelics themselves, and attention is focused on fentanyl instead. With underground ceremonies, especially for newcomers, it's key to ask the right questions: how much experience do you have with this medicine, how much medicine are you serving, what's the group size, is there a vetting process, are you trauma-informed, do you offer prep and integration. Interviewing whoever you work with — retreat center, underground provider, therapist, or coach — is essential.

Kellan: With California potentially legalizing, what do you envision a fully legal psychedelic market looking like — like cannabis, or more through certified providers like ketamine clinics?

Paul F. Austin: Cannabis actually isn't federally legal — hemp is technically federally legal, but cannabis itself is a state-driven, grassroots shift, even more grassroots than the psychedelic movement, which has pros and cons — a lot of that grassroots push wasn't informed by scientific practice, and we're seeing some challenges now; I've personally experienced cannabis addiction, for better or worse. With psychedelics, I think MDMA will be approved by the FDA to treat PTSD very likely this year, with rollout around December 2024 or January 2025. Psilocybin, the alkaloid in magic mushrooms, will likely be legalized by the FDA with rollout around 2027, for treatment-resistant depression and major depressive disorder. I'd guess five to ten other psychedelics — microdose LSD for depression, psilocybin analogs for depression, potentially ibogaine for certain addictions — could be FDA approved before the end of the decade. The challenge is a lot of regulation, high cost, and it's unclear if insurance will cover it since many treatments require a therapist present, unlike a daily SSRI pill. My guess is about 10% of people who work with psychedelics will do so through that FDA-approved path over the next ten years. The majority will work with psychedelics either through a state model like Colorado, Oregon, or potentially California, or through a more localized community church model with religious protection as part of a nonprofit, low cost, some vetting but not cost-prohibitive — that's currently legal in Colorado, where you can't sell mushrooms but can donate them as part of a retreat or ceremony. I think 80-90% of use will occur in that community church model, and the state-licensed model sits somewhere between FDA approval and the community church model, with licensed facilitators who don't need to be clinicians.

Kellan: Are there certain groups of people, from an age or life-stage perspective, who benefit most from retreats — and conversely, is there a window where it's likely not the best time?

Paul F. Austin: The main contraindication for psychedelic use is schizophrenia — someone with schizophrenia or a family history of it, especially under 26, should not work with psychedelics, probably not cannabis either, and should be very careful. Someone on lithium should also avoid psilocybin in particular — that's really the main contraindication. Also, if someone has had a very recent traumatizing experience — say a parent passed away a week before a planned retreat — it's probably better to push the retreat out until they feel more internally stable. As for who benefits most — and this may be controversial — very young adults, 16 to 19, doing this as an intentional rite of passage, like a men's circle or with a parent or community, can be incredibly beneficial; my own LSD experiences at 19 were very positive and completely changed the trajectory of my life. There is real risk though — family mental health history needs to be clearly understood, and dosing should step up gradually so you can gauge response. It's more risky than doing this in your 50s or 60s, but psychedelics are by far the safest way to have a rite of passage or initiation compared to traditional indigenous initiations, which were often physically dangerous. The other group that benefits most is people in their 50s and 60s who've been stuck in their ways for a long time, at a midlife crisis or entering retirement, looking for a new sense of vitality — Michael Pollan said something similar in How to Change Your Mind. Psychedelics can help reframe how we approach pain and death; something like 95% of healthcare spending happens in the last year of someone's life, largely because we don't know how to die as a culture, and psychedelics can help us remember death is a transition, not a jail sentence.

Bryan Fields: I love it, Paul. We only have time for one more question. I take you to the mountains, drop you off, give you 200 micrograms of LSD, and you can bring three people, dead or alive — who are you bringing?

Paul F. Austin: I'm assuming you follow me on Twitter since I saw you followed me the other day. I had a tweet a few months ago about how one of my favorite things to do is take 200 mics of LSD and go on a mountain, which I do once every few years. Number one would be Stewart Brand — an OG in Silicon Valley tech psychedelic culture, part of Ken Kesey's Merry Pranksters in the 60s, did LSD with Jim Fadiman back in the day, started the Acid Tests with the Grateful Dead, started the Whole Earth Catalog, came up with the idea of seeing a picture of Earth from space which helped kick off Earth Day and the ecological movement. He was influential at the bridge between counterculture and cyberculture, still alive — I've tweeted at him recently trying to link up. His most recent project is de-extinction, trying to bring woolly mammoths back to help with climate change; there's a documentary about him called We Are As Gods, from his quote in the Whole Earth Catalog, "We are as gods, so we might as well get good at it." He was close friends with Kevin Kelly, who started Wired, and Brian Eno. Second person would be Leonardo da Vinci — inventor, artist, the original Renaissance man, which is something I aspire to, having both creativity and craftsmanship. I've read parts of his biography by Walter Isaacson. Third would be Aldous Huxley, probably my favorite author — wrote Brave New World in 1933, very dystopian and cynical, came from a wealthy upper-class Oxford family, and World War II opened up a spiritual crisis for him; he started studying Vedanta and then experimented with mescaline and LSD, and just before he died wrote a utopian counterpart to Brave New World called Island. The coolest part is that on his deathbed he had his wife inject him with 100 micrograms of LSD, so he was tripping on acid while dying, which is basically what I think all of us should aspire to. So Stewart Brand, Leonardo da Vinci, and Aldous Huxley — those would be my three.

Bryan Fields: I love it. So for our listeners, where can they find you if they want to get in touch and learn more?

faq.answer: According to Paul Austin, a high-dose psychedelic experience typically creates a 2-3 week window of increased flow, compassion, and openness; microdosing afterward can extend that window to 6-8 weeks, which is roughly the time needed to establish a lasting new habit.

faq.question: Which age groups benefit most from psychedelic retreats?
faq.answer: Austin points to two groups: young adults (16-19) using psychedelics as an intentional rite of passage, and adults in their 50s-60s who feel stuck in long-standing patterns and are seeking renewed vitality or a shift in perspective around aging and mortality.
